source_refs.note: Book p. 188-190: 6.4 Ellipse, definition, Kepler's first law, Figure 6.14, Derivation of the Standard Equation with Figure 6.15, Do You Know box

blocks.text: An ellipse is the set of all points in a plane for which the sum of distances from two fixed points, called the foci (plural of focus), is constant (see Figure 14). Kepler's first law states that the orbits of the planets in the solar system are elliptical.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says "see Figure 14". The figure it means is Figure 6.14 (below).

blocks.alt: An ellipse with two foci F' and F on its long axis. Two different points P on the ellipse are each joined to both foci; for each P the two joining segments together have the same total length.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.14: the sum |PF'| + |PF| is the same for every point P (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Picture it with a loop of thread: fix two pins (the foci) on a board, put a loop of thread around them, pull it tight with a pencil and move the pencil all the way round. The thread length never changes, so the pencil always keeps the sum of its distances to the two pins the same. The curve it draws is an ellipse.
In Figure 6.14 the red pair of segments and the green pair of segments look different, but each pair adds up to the same total length. That one fixed total is the whole definition.
Kepler's law in simple words: a planet does not go round the Sun in a perfect circle; it goes round on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

To obtain the simplest equation for an ellipse, we place the foci on the x-axis at the points \(F'(-c, 0)\) and \(F(c, 0)\), so that the origin is the midpoint of the segment joining them (see Figure 17). Let the constant sum of distances from any point \(P(x, y)\) on the ellipse to the foci be \(2a\), where \(a > 0\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says "see Figure 17" here and again in "triangle PF'F in Figure 17" further down. Both times the figure it means is Figure 6.15 (below).

blocks.alt: Ellipse centred at the origin O with foci F'(-c, 0) and F(c, 0) on the x-axis; a point P(x, y) on the ellipse is joined to both foci.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.15: foci at F'(-c, 0) and F(c, 0), point P(x, y) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why put the foci at \((\pm c, 0)\)? Choosing the axes this way puts the centre at the origin and makes the ellipse symmetric about both axes, so the final equation has no \(x\)-term, no \(y\)-term and no \(xy\)-term. Any other ellipse is just this one moved (Theorems 1 and 2 in 6.4.2).
Why call the sum \(2a\) and not just \(a\)? Because \(a\) will turn out to be the distance from the centre to a vertex; the factor 2 keeps the final formula clean.
Thus, for any point \(P(x, y)\) on the ellipse,

blocks.text_alt: distance P F dash plus distance P F equals 2 a

blocks.text:
Using the distance formula,
\[\sqrt{(x+c)^2+y^2} + \sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\]
\[= 2a\]
To simplify, isolate one radical and square both sides:
\[\sqrt{(x+c)^2+y^2}\]
\[= 2a - \sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\]
Squaring,
\[(x+c)^2+y^2\]
\[= 4a^2 - 4a\sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\]
\[\qquad + (x-c)^2 + y^2\]
Expanding the squares,
\[x^2+2cx+c^2+y^2\]
\[= 4a^2 - 4a\sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\]
\[\qquad + x^2-2cx+c^2+y^2\]
Cancelling the common terms \(x^2\), \(c^2\), and \(y^2\) from both sides,
\[2cx = 4a^2 - 4a\sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2} - 2cx\]
Bring the terms involving \(cx\) together:
\[4cx = 4a^2 - 4a\sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\]
Divide by 4 and isolate the remaining radical:
\[a\sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2} = a^2 - cx\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: After the line \(\sqrt{(x+c)^2+y^2} = 2a - \sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\) the book prints a stray radical sign \(\sqrt{\ }\) at the end of the line. It is a printing mistake and has no meaning; the equation ends at \(\sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why isolate one radical before squaring? If we square \(\sqrt{A} + \sqrt{B} = 2a\) directly we get \(A + B + 2\sqrt{AB} = 4a^2\), and the product \(\sqrt{AB}\) is worse than before. With one root on each side, squaring removes the left root completely and leaves only one root on the right.
Squaring the right side uses \((p - q)^2 = p^2 - 2pq + q^2\) with \(p = 2a\) and \(q = \sqrt{(x-c)^2+y^2}\): this gives \(4a^2 - 4a\sqrt{\ldots} + (x-c)^2 + y^2\).
After the first squaring one radical is still left, so we isolate it and square a second time.

Now we square both sides again:
\[a^2\left[(x-c)^2+y^2\right]\]
\[= a^4 - 2a^2cx + c^2x^2\]
Expanding the left side:
\[a^2(x^2-2cx+c^2+y^2)\]
\[= a^4 - 2a^2cx + c^2x^2\]
\[a^2x^2 - 2a^2cx + a^2c^2 + a^2y^2\]
\[= a^4 - 2a^2cx + c^2x^2\]
\[a^2x^2 + a^2c^2 + a^2y^2 = a^4 + c^2x^2\]
Rearranging,
\[a^2x^2 - c^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^4 - a^2c^2\]
\[(a^2-c^2)x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2(a^2-c^2)\]

From triangle \(PF'F\) in Figure 17, we note that \(|PF'| + |PF| > |F'F|\), that is, \(2a > 2c\), so \(a > c\) and thus \(a^2 - c^2 > 0\). For convenience, we define a new constant \(b\) such that \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(2a > 2c\)? In any triangle, two sides together are longer than the third side. Here the two sides \(PF'\) and \(PF\) add up to \(2a\), and the third side \(F'F\) has length \(2c\).
Why introduce \(b\)? Only to make the equation neat. Since \(a^2 - c^2\) is positive, it is the square of some positive number; we call that number \(b\). Later you will see that \(b\) is the distance from the centre to the ends of the short axis.

Substituting, the equation of the ellipse becomes
\[b^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2b^2\]
Finally, dividing both sides by \(a^2b^2\) gives the standard form of the equation of an ellipse:

blocks.text_alt: x squared over a squared plus y squared over b squared equals 1

blocks.text: Since \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\) and \(a > c\), it follows that \(a > b\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
An ellipse: the sum of the distances of every point from the two foci is the same constant \(2a\).
With foci \((\pm c, 0)\), the equation is \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\), where \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2\).
Always \(a > c\) and \(a > b\): \(a\) is the largest of the three lengths.
The derivation uses two squarings, each time after isolating one radical.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Writing \(b^2 = a^2 + c^2\) (that is the hyperbola relation). For an ellipse, \(c^2 = a^2 - b^2\), so \(c\) is smaller than \(a\).
Squaring \(\sqrt{A} + \sqrt{B}\) as \(A + B\): the middle term \(2\sqrt{AB}\) is always there. That is why we isolate one radical first.
